BioNTech's BNT122 program - individualized mRNA neoantigen vaccines
The National Cancer Institute's neoantigen T-cell therapy program
Sipuleucel-T (Provenge) - the first FDA-approved therapeutic cancer vaccine, 2010
how: A tumor sample is sequenced to identify neoantigens - mutated protein fragments unique to that patient's cancer. Algorithms predict which neoantigens the immune system can recognize, and a vaccine (often mRNA) encoding up to 34 of them is manufactured for that individual. Injected, the vaccine trains T cells to hunt cells displaying those mutations. The approach is usually combined with checkpoint inhibitors that release the immune system's brakes. Each vaccine is made for one patient - true personalization.
name: Personalized Cancer Vaccines
principles: Neoantigens are the target: mutations unique to the tumor make the most specific vaccine targets.
Prediction is the bottleneck: algorithms must guess which mutations the immune system will see.
Speed matters: manufacturing must go from biopsy to injection in weeks, not months.
Combinations win: vaccines plus checkpoint inhibitors outperform either alone.
Personalization is the product: each vaccine is manufactured for one patient.

public.i: Coley's toxins were the first evidence that the immune system could fight cancer - the founding observation.
public.k: New York surgeon William Coley noticed that cancer patients who developed severe bacterial infections sometimes saw their tumors shrink, and in the 1890s he began injecting bacterial toxins - Coley's toxins - to provoke immune responses against sarcomas. Some patients responded dramatically. The work was uncontrolled by modern standards, but it planted the founding idea: immunity can attack cancer.
public.srcn: Coley W.B., 1890s case series; histories of cancer immunotherapy.
public.title: Coley's Toxins: The First Cancer Immunotherapy

public.i: Ehrlich's magic bullet framed the goal: treatments that strike disease and spare the patient.
public.k: Paul Ehrlich proposed the magic bullet concept in the early 1900s - therapies that target disease specifically while sparing healthy tissue. Though aimed at infections, the idea shaped cancer thinking for a century: the ideal cancer treatment would distinguish tumor from self. Personalized vaccines are Ehrlich's bullet, guided by the tumor's own mutations.
public.srcn: Ehrlich P., magic bullet concept; history of chemotherapy.
public.title: Ehrlich's Magic Bullet: The Targeting Dream

public.i: Immune surveillance proposed that the body already fights cancer daily - vaccines would amplify a natural process.
public.k: Frank Macfarlane Burnet and Lewis Thomas proposed the immune surveillance hypothesis in 1957: the immune system constantly detects and destroys emerging cancer cells, and tumors are the ones that escape. The hypothesis implied that strengthening immune recognition - exactly what vaccines do - was a legitimate cancer strategy. It took decades of evidence to confirm the mechanism.
public.srcn: Burnet F.M., 1957; Thomas L., 1959; immune surveillance literature.
public.title: Immune Surveillance: The Body Already Fights

public.i: BCG proved immune stimulation could treat human cancer - the first modern immunotherapy success.
public.k: In 1976, Alvaro Morales reported that BCG - the tuberculosis vaccine - instilled into the bladder treated superficial bladder cancer, and it became standard therapy. The mechanism was crude immune activation, not specific targeting. But BCG's success proved the principle in a controlled trial: stimulating immunity treats real human cancers.
public.srcn: Morales A. et al., 1976; BCG bladder-cancer trial literature.
public.title: BCG for Bladder Cancer: Immunity Proves Itself

public.i: Interferons and interleukins showed immune molecules had anti-tumor activity - and harsh limits.
public.k: Through the 1980s, interferon-alpha and interleukin-2 were tested against cancers, with occasional dramatic responses in melanoma and kidney cancer - and severe toxicity. The cytokines proved immune activation could shrink tumors but were too blunt for most patients. The field learned it needed specificity, not just stimulation.
public.title: Cytokines: Power Without Precision

public.i: MAGE-A1 gave cancer vaccines their first defined molecular target.
public.k: Pierre van der Bruggen's team identified MAGE-A1 in 1991 - the first human tumor antigen recognized by T cells, found on melanomas but not normal tissues (except testis). For the first time, a vaccine could aim at a defined tumor molecule. MAGE vaccines entered trials; the responses were modest, but the target paradigm was established.
public.srcn: Van der Bruggen et al., Science, 1991.
public.title: MAGE-A1: The First Defined Tumor Antigen

public.i: The 1990s taught the field that shared antigens were not enough - the target had to be personal.
public.k: Through the 1990s, cancer vaccines targeting shared tumor antigens - MAGE, gp100, NY-ESO-1 - entered clinical trials with disappointing results: immune responses, but rarely tumor shrinkage. The lesson was humbling: tumors are too individual for one-size-fits-all vaccines. The failures redirected the field toward the mutations unique to each patient.
public.title: Shared Antigens Disappoint: The Personal Turn

public.i: Exome sequencing made the personal turn technically possible: every tumor's mutations, readable.
public.k: Cheap DNA sequencing in the 2000s let researchers read a tumor's full exome - all its protein-coding mutations - revealing that each cancer carries dozens to hundreds of unique neoantigens. Vogelstein and others showed these mutations were the immune system's best targets. The technology to find personal targets finally existed.
public.srcn: Cancer genome sequencing literature; Vogelstein lab publications, 2000s.
public.title: Exome Sequencing Reveals Each Tumor's Mutations

public.i: Provenge's approval proved regulators would approve a therapeutic cancer vaccine - the pathway existed.
public.k: The FDA approved sipuleucel-T (Provenge) in 2010 for prostate cancer - the first therapeutic cancer vaccine, made from the patient's own immune cells. The survival benefit was modest (about 4 months) and the product was commercially troubled. But Provenge proved the regulatory pathway: personalized immune therapies could be approved.
public.srcn: FDA approval records, 2010; Provenge trial publications.
public.title: Provenge Approved: The Regulatory Pathway Opens
Ipilimumab: The First Checkpoint Drug
public.k: The FDA approved ipilimumab (Yervoy) in 2011 - the first checkpoint inhibitor, blocking CTLA-4 to unleash T cells against melanoma. The drug extended survival but with significant autoimmune side effects. It proved the checkpoint concept in humans and set the stage for the PD-1 revolution.
public.i: Ipilimumab proved checkpoint blockade works in humans - the concept behind every vaccine combination.
public.srcn: FDA approval records, 2011; ipilimumab trial literature.

public.i: mRNA matured as a programmable vaccine platform - the delivery vehicle personalized vaccines needed.
public.k: Through the early 2010s, researchers at BioNTech, Moderna, and universities solved mRNA's delivery and stability problems - lipid nanoparticles, modified nucleosides (Karikó and Weissman). mRNA could encode any protein, be manufactured quickly, and be redesigned in software. The platform was ready; it needed a target. Neoantigens were waiting.
public.srcn: mRNA platform literature; Karikó and Weissman publications.
public.title: mRNA Becomes a Programmable Platform

public.i: The first personalized neoantigen vaccines were made and injected - dendritic cells carrying personal mutations.
public.k: In 2012-2014, pioneering teams - at Washington University, the NCI, and elsewhere - manufactured the first truly personalized neoantigen vaccines: dendritic cells loaded with a patient's own tumor mutations. Early melanoma trials showed T-cell responses against the personal targets. The manufacturing was artisanal and slow, but the concept worked in humans.
public.title: The First Personalized Neoantigen Vaccines

public.i: Rosenberg's NCI team showed neoantigen-targeted T cells could shrink tumors - the biological proof.
public.k: Steven Rosenberg's team at the National Cancer Institute demonstrated in 2014 that T cells targeting a patient's neoantigens could cause tumor regression - including in a cholangiocarcinoma patient. The result proved neoantigens were not just markers but actionable immune targets. The biology was real; the challenge was manufacturing at scale.
public.title: NCI: Neoantigen T Cells Shrink Tumors

public.i: Checkpoint inhibitors changed the context: vaccines would have a powerful combination partner.
public.k: PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors - pembrolizumab, nivolumab - transformed oncology from 2015, releasing the immune system's brakes with unprecedented response rates in melanoma and lung cancer. But many patients still did not respond. The field saw the combination logic immediately: vaccines to aim the immune system, checkpoint drugs to unleash it.
public.srcn: PD-1 inhibitor trial literature, 2015; FDA approvals.
public.title: Checkpoint Inhibitors Transform Oncology

public.i: BioNTech and Moderna launched neoantigen programs - the mRNA giants entered personalized cancer.
public.k: In 2016, BioNTech and Moderna - then known for infectious-disease mRNA - launched personalized cancer vaccine programs, encoding patient-specific neoantigens in mRNA. The manufacturing pitch was compelling: sequence the tumor, design the mRNA in software, manufacture in weeks. Pharma's mRNA infrastructure pivoted to oncology.
public.title: The mRNA Giants Enter Neoantigens
The Cancer Moonshot Funds Neoantigens
public.k: The US Cancer Moonshot initiative, launched in 2016, directed major funding toward immunotherapy including neoantigen research. Federal money accelerated the academic programs that fed the biotech pipelines. The Moonshot's emphasis on data sharing also built the genomic datasets prediction algorithms needed.
public.i: Federal Moonshot funding accelerated academic neoantigen programs and their datasets.
CAR-T approvals proved engineered immune cells were a real drug class - the field's confidence soared.
public.k: The FDA approved the first CAR-T cell therapies in 2017 - Kymriah and Yescarta - engineered immune cells that produced remissions in blood cancers. Though a different technology, CAR-T's success validated the entire engineered-immunity enterprise, including vaccines. Investors and regulators now believed immune engineering was medicine, not science fiction.
public.title: CAR-T Approved: Engineered Immunity Validated

public.i: First mRNA neoantigen trial results showed personal vaccines generate personal T cells.
public.k: Early-phase trials of mRNA neoantigen vaccines through 2017-2019 - Moderna's mRNA-4157, BioNTech's BNT122 - showed the vaccines were safe and generated T-cell responses against the encoded personal mutations. The immunology worked as designed. Efficacy data was still early, but the mechanism was confirmed in humans.
public.title: mRNA Neoantigen Trials: The Immune Response Confirmed

public.i: COVID mRNA vaccines validated the platform at planetary scale - manufacturing, safety, speed.
public.k: The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines - Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna - were developed, tested, and deployed to billions in 2020, validating mRNA manufacturing, safety databases, and rapid redesign at unprecedented scale. The platform that would carry personalized cancer vaccines had just passed the largest clinical trial in history. Public trust and manufacturing capacity followed.
public.srcn: COVID-19 mRNA vaccine trial and deployment records, 2020.
public.title: COVID Validates the mRNA Platform

public.i: The mRNA-4157 plus Keytruda combination trials expanded - the pivotal combination took shape.
public.k: Through 2021, Moderna and Merck expanded trials combining mRNA-4157 (encoding up to 34 personal neoantigens) with pembrolizumab (Keytruda) in melanoma and other cancers. The combination logic - vaccine aims, checkpoint unleashes - was now in definitive testing. Enrollment in the randomized phase 2b trial completed, setting up the field's most important readout.
public.title: The Pivotal Combination Takes Shape

public.i: Phase 2 melanoma data showed a 44 percent reduction in recurrence risk - the field's breakthrough readout.
public.k: In late 2022, Moderna and Merck reported phase 2b results: mRNA-4157 plus Keytruda reduced melanoma recurrence or death risk by 44 percent versus Keytruda alone. It was the first randomized evidence that a personalized cancer vaccine improves outcomes. The stock market noticed; more importantly, oncology did. The breakthrough was real but needed phase 3 confirmation.
public.title: The 44 Percent Readout: Breakthrough Data

public.i: Phase 3 launched and BioNTech's pancreatic data showed the approach reaching hard cancers.
public.k: In 2023, the phase 3 trial of mRNA-4157 plus Keytruda in melanoma began enrolling, while BioNTech reported that its BNT122 neoantigen vaccine generated T-cell responses in pancreatic cancer - one of oncology's hardest targets. The field was now testing personalized vaccines in the cancers that needed them most. Multiple phase 3 programs were underway.
public.srcn: Phase 3 trial initiations; BioNTech pancreatic data, 2023.
public.title: Phase 3 Begins; Pancreatic Signals

public.i: Phase 3 programs expanded to lung cancer - the biggest solid-tumor prize.
public.k: Through 2024, personalized vaccine phase 3 programs expanded: mRNA-4157 trials in non-small cell lung cancer and other indications enrolled, while Transgene's TG4050 and others reported head-and-neck data. Manufacturing timelines compressed toward the weeks-long target. The field was running multiple shots on goal across cancer types.
public.title: Phase 3 Expands: Lung Cancer and Beyond
ctDNA Guides Vaccine Timing
public.k: Through 2024, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) testing matured to the point of guiding vaccine trials: detecting microscopic residual disease to select patients and measuring response. The liquid-biopsy pairing gave vaccines a timing instrument - treat when ctDNA appears, not before. Precision timing joined precision targeting.
public.i: Liquid biopsies gave personalized vaccines a timing instrument.
AI neoantigen prediction improved markedly - better algorithms, better targets.
public.k: Machine-learning models for predicting which tumor mutations will provoke immunity - MHC binding, T-cell recognition - improved substantially through 2024, trained on growing immunopeptidomics datasets. Better prediction means better vaccines: the right 34 neoantigens instead of plausible guesses. The computational half of personalization was catching up to the sequencing half.
public.title: AI Sharpens Neoantigen Prediction

public.i: Individualized manufacturing scaled toward industrial timelines - weeks from biopsy to vial.
public.k: Through 2025, manufacturers industrialized the personalized pipeline: automated sequencing, AI-driven neoantigen selection, and rapid mRNA production compressing biopsy-to-vaccine timelines toward 4-6 weeks. The artisanal era ended; the industrial era began. Manufacturing at scale was the precondition for phase 3 success becoming clinical reality.
public.title: Manufacturing Scales: Biopsy to Vial in Weeks

public.i: Adjuvant trials tested vaccines where they may matter most: after surgery, against microscopic disease.
public.k: In 2025, personalized vaccine trials expanded into the adjuvant setting - treating patients after tumor removal, when only microscopic disease remains and the immune system has the best chance. The logic was compelling: vaccines work best against small targets. Adjuvant success would move vaccines earlier in treatment, where the benefit could be largest.
public.title: Adjuvant Trials: Treating Microscopic Disease

public.i: The phase 3 melanoma readout is the most anticipated result in cancer vaccines - the verdict on personalization.
public.k: The phase 3 trial of mRNA-4157 plus Keytruda in resected melanoma - the INTerpath program - approached its primary readout in 2025-2026, testing whether the 44 percent phase 2 signal holds at scale. A positive readout would likely bring the first personalized cancer vaccine to market. The field held its breath: this trial validates or refutes the entire approach.
public.srcn: Clinical trial registries; INTerpath program disclosures.
public.title: The Phase 3 Verdict Approaches

public.i: Regulators built frameworks for one-patient drugs - approval for N-of-1 manufacturing.
public.k: Through 2026, the FDA and EMA developed regulatory frameworks for individualized therapies - approving the manufacturing process and neoantigen-selection algorithm rather than a fixed product. The N-of-1 regulatory model was unprecedented: each dose differs, but the process is validated. The frameworks will govern the whole personalized-medicine era.
public.title: Regulating the N-of-1 Drug

public.i: Cost and access emerged as the defining challenge: personalization is expensive.
public.k: By 2026, the economics were stark: personalized vaccines cost tens of thousands per patient to manufacture, raising questions about access and reimbursement. Health systems debated how to pay for N-of-1 therapies. The field's next challenge was not biological but economic: making personalization affordable enough to matter at population scale.
public.title: The Access Challenge: Paying for Personal

public.i: Off-the-shelf shared neoantigen vaccines offered a cheaper complement to fully personal ones.
public.k: Through 2026, developers advanced off-the-shelf vaccines targeting shared neoantigens - common driver mutations like KRAS variants - that could treat many patients without personalization. The shared vaccines traded precision for scale and cost. The field converged on a portfolio: personal vaccines for maximum precision, shared vaccines for maximum reach.
public.title: Shared Neoantigens: The Off-the-Shelf Complement

public.i: Combination science matured: vaccines plus checkpoints plus T-cell therapies in rational sequences.
public.k: By 2026, trial designs combined personalized vaccines with checkpoint inhibitors, TIL therapy, and other modalities in rational sequences - priming with vaccines, expanding with cells, unleashing with checkpoints. The combinations reflected a maturing science: no single modality wins alone. The future is orchestrated immunity.
public.title: Orchestrated Immunity: Rational Combinations

public.i: The frontier, honestly stated: advanced trials, real signals, no approved product yet - the evidence status.
public.k: As of 2026, personalized cancer vaccines stand at an honest frontier: phase 3 trials underway, phase 2 signals genuinely promising, manufacturing industrializing - but no personalized cancer vaccine yet approved, and the phase 3 verdict still pending. Some approaches have reached advanced clinical trials, as documented throughout this record. This database records the evidence as it stands: promising, unproven at scale, and moving fast.
public.srcn: Synthesis of trial registries and company disclosures current to 2026.
public.title: The Frontier, Honestly Stated

public.i: Research horizons: early-interception studies and preventive concepts are in early testing - evidence pending.
public.k: Research directions as of 2026 include early-interception studies - vaccinating high-risk individuals before cancer develops - and preventive concepts for hereditary cancer syndromes. These are early research, not established approaches: trials are small and evidence is preliminary. The horizon is scientifically exciting and evidentially thin - exactly what the frontier label means.
public.title: Research Horizons: Interception and Prevention

status_note: Emerging - some approaches have reached advanced clinical trials (phase 2/3); no personalized cancer vaccine is approved as of 2026; evidence status labeled on every record. This database describes research, not medical advice.
what: Personalized cancer vaccines are treatments designed around the mutations in an individual patient's tumor: the tumor is sequenced, its unique neoantigens are identified, and a vaccine - often mRNA - is manufactured to train that patient's immune system to recognize those mutations. It matters because every tumor is genetically distinct, and a vaccine built from the tumor's own mutations offers a level of specificity no off-the-shelf drug can match.
why: Cancer remains one of humanity's leading causes of death, and conventional treatments - surgery, radiation, chemotherapy - are blunt instruments with harsh side effects. Immunotherapy has already transformed outcomes for some cancers, but many patients do not respond. Personalized vaccines aim to extend immunotherapy's reach by aiming the immune system precisely at each patient's tumor. Some approaches have reached advanced clinical trials.
